articles.title: Tempe Union parents question district amid voyeurism charges
articles.description: An employee of Tempe Union High School District is facing voyeurism charges after police said he misused school security footage to spy on undressed girls. Prosecutors say Antony Cruz, 28, downloaded videos of female students in a changing room at Corona del Sol High School. Parents spoke out after a Tempe Union High School District security officer was accused of spying on female students while they undressed in a makeshift changing room. A number of parents spoke at a Sept. 2 school board meeting, calling on the district to increase safety procedures and transparency with families. Prosecutors say Antony Cruz, 28, downloaded videos of female students in a changing room at Corona del Sol High School in south Tempe. The district said girls were changing in a dance room while the locker room was undergoing renovations. Police believe cameras in the makeshift changing room were "inadvertently" left on. Arizona does not have a law that mandates security cameras in schools. Tracy Pearl, a technology and law professor at Arizona State University, previously told The Republic the dance room essentially became a de facto room because the girls were instructed to change in it. That means the school would have been legally required to ensure there were no cameras in the room or obtain consent from the students being recorded or their parents. One parent, Ben Zorensky, questioned why the district had a camera in the room when it prohibits cameras in changing areas. Because the camera was installed in 2024, Zorensky also questioned whether other female students could have been potential victims. Another parent, Cecilia Trevizo, questioned why the district did not inform parents that students were being recorded and that cameras had been installed in multiple dance rooms. Trevizo said a staff member previously asked for the camera to be removed because of the dancers' privacy concerns. She questioned why a camera was installed in a dance room in the first place. Trevizo also said another security guard insisted the camera remain because of concerns that students were skipping class. "There were multiple opportunities to stop this," Trevizo said. "There were multiple opportunities to protect these students, and these opportunities were missed." Trevizo called on the governing board to hold district leadership accountable for failing to keep the children safe, and to conduct a third-party investigation into who requested the cameras and who approved their installation. Another parent said he's unsure if his daughter may have been a victim and has received limited information from the district. While the district previously said Tempe police had identified all victims, it released a statement to parents on Aug. 31 indicating police now believed there were more victims. Have a news tip? Contact The Arizona Republic and azcentral.com at newstips@arizonarepublic.com.

articles.title: Ex-Tempe school employee scheduled to appear in court on voyeurism charges
articles.description: TEMPE, AZ (AZFamily) -- A former school surveillance officer is scheduled to appear in court after authorities say he downloaded footage that showed underage girls undressing at an East Valley high school. Antony Cruz, 28, is slated to be arraigned before a judge at 8:30 a.m. Thursday. District says room was not for changing Cruz, who worked as a surveillance officer for the Tempe Union High School District, allegedly gained access to cameras that were recording a room of young teen girls undressing at Corona del Sol High School. Police noted in the court paperwork that staff and students requested the cameras be turned off for privacy, but were left on and recording the room. Authorities said Cruz did not notify school staff or law enforcement of the camera exposing the girls. Instead, Cruz reportedly downloaded several videos, with at least seven showing young girls' changing in and out of their clothes. Court documents state that the room was being used temporarily as a changing room for students because the girls' locker room was closed for renovations. District officials said the space is a dance room, not a locker room, and was never designated by the district as a place for students to change clothes. During recent locker room renovations, the district said it approved a request from Corona del Sol High School to set up a separate, camera-free location for students to change. Officials said the dance room was not one of the approved locations. A security camera was installed in the room in 2024 for campus safety purposes. Parents react at school board meeting Parents who spoke at Wednesday night's school board meeting were visibly upset, wondering if their children are victims. "He's been charged with seven counts of voyeurism, but I believe from this long, almost one-month period, that there are many more counts he should be charged with, and so I ask the district please disclose this information so we can find out the full breadth of the victims," one parent said. The district has opened an internal investigation into the matter. Cruz is facing seven counts of voyeurism and is being held on a $100,000 cash-only bond. articles.title: Class action filed over Ruby Memorial hidden cameras
articles.description: MORGANTOWN - A Monongalia County woman has filed a proposed class-action lawsuit over hidden cameras found in staff bathrooms at Ruby Memorial Hospital. The plaintiff, identified in the complaint only as P.J.P., filed the complaint September 1 in Monongalia Circuit Court. West Virginia University Hospitals and West Virginia United Health System are the named defendants. "A hospital restroom should be an unquestioned sanctuary of privacy, not a crime scene with a hidden lens," Troy Giatras, one of the attorneys who filed the complaint, told The West Virginia Record. "These dedicated healthcare workers came to work to save lives, only to have their fundamental dignity violated." In the complaint, P.J.P. alleges she was a Ruby Memorial employee during the relevant period and was among workers secretly recorded in staff restroom facilities. She says the defendants failed to protect employees from hidden-camera surveillance in nonpublic staff bathrooms. She alleges the entities were negligent and grossly negligent in hiring, supervising, training and retaining employees, including former physician Lance Parks, and in maintaining a workplace protected from invasions of privacy. According to the complaint, a staff member found a hidden recording device June 26 beneath a sink in a nonpublic staff restroom at Ruby Memorial. A second device was discovered July 1 after a facilities employee responded to a clogged toilet in another nonpublic restroom, the suit says. Authorities previously said the first device contained footage of eight hospital employees who were unknowingly recorded while partially nude. The second device contained no images or other media, according to the Monongalia County Prosecutor's Office. The complaint alleges Parks "surreptitiously recorded nude and/or partially nude employees" in the nonpublic bathrooms and the defendants did not adequately protect staff members from the alleged surveillance. "While law enforcement handles the criminal conduct of Lance Parks, the civil justice system exists to hold institutions accountable for failing their duty of care," Matt Stonestreet, another attorney representing the plaintiffs, told The Record. "WVU Hospitals provided the venue, employed the physician, and assured staff their private spaces were safe. "When an institution fails to supervise its staff and conducts sweeps that miss hidden cameras right under its nose, it shares full legal and moral responsibility for the harm caused." The complaint further alleges the hospitals failed to detect the devices, including after the first camera was found. The defendants initially suspended the employee involved and later said he no longer worked at the hospital, according to reports. Parks was charged in July with eight misdemeanor counts of criminal invasion of privacy and one felony count involving the distribution and exhibition of computer-generated child pornography, according to the Monongalia County Prosecutor's Office. Investigators executed a search warrant at his home and seized computers and digital-storage devices for forensic examination. Investigators said they were continuing to examine the seized devices to determine the full scope of potential criminal conduct and identify any additional victims. The civil complaint says Parks waived his preliminary hearing and is awaiting possible indictment by the Monongalia County Prosecutor's Office. "WVU Hospitals told staff they swept the facilities and found nothing," Giatras told The Record. "Days later, plumbing backed up and a second camera was pulled from a toilet. That is not thorough security. That is negligent indifference. "Once these deeply intimate, non-consensual recordings exist, they cannot be unseen. The psychological damage follows these victims every single day." The plaintiff contends the alleged conduct was gender-based harassment and discrimination because she is a woman and asserts the cameras were installed to secretly record women "when they were the most vulnerable." The complaint accuses the defendants of invasion of privacy, breach of confidentiality, violations of the West Virginia Human Rights Act, violation of the West Virginia Constitution, negligent supervision, negligent infliction of emotional distress, violation of the West Virginia Wiretapping and Electronic Surveillance Act and negligence. "You cannot shrug off corporate responsibility by blaming one bad actor when your own policies, supervision, and facility checks completely collapsed," Giatras said. The complaint also alleges the defendants' conduct caused anxiety, humiliation, emotional distress, pain and suffering, mental anguish, loss of enjoyment of life, annoyance and inconvenience. It seeks class certification for West Virginia residents allegedly recorded in nonpublic bathroom facilities at Ruby Memorial and "any other facility" owned, operated or managed by the defendants in the state. The plaintiff and potential class seek compensatory and punitive damages, attorney fees, court costs and class certification. The lawsuit was filed by Giatras and Stonestreet of The Giatras Law Firm in Charleston. The case has been assigned to Circuit Judge Perri J. DeChristopher. Giatras said any additional victims confidentially can contact his firm for more information by texting 304-343-2900 or visiting its website. Monongalia Circuit Court case number 26-C-347

pendingReview.title: In China, grassroots investigators work to stop illicitly recorded adult content
pendingReview.description: Zhou Ninghe was browsing the internet one day when he saw a surveillance video of a changing room, showing several women undressing and showering. At first, he assumed the video was staged, the type of soft-core pornography that can occasionally slip past the automated systems that power much of China's tough internet controls, before a human censor spots and deletes it. But then he recognized the venue, a popular water park near his home in Fuzhou. A corporate fraud investigator, Mr. Zhou began digging and soon discovered the video was the tip of a sordid iceberg of stolen and illicitly recorded content, much of it traded and sold in private chat groups. Over the next three months, he spent most of his spare time downloading videos and compiling evidence, building around 10 cases with identifiable perpetrators and filing reports with the police, but nothing came of it. "Frustrated by the lack of progress through official channels, I decided to expose the footage publicly online instead," Mr. Zhou said. "Within a single month of posting, one perpetrator was arrested." Pornography is illegal in China, with potential prison terms for those found guilty of producing or distributing sexual content for profit. Popular online porn sites, such as those operated by Montreal-based Aylo, are all censored by the Great Firewall. But just as critics of anti-pornography age-verification laws have warned could happen in the West, blocking mainstream websites has created a booming, unregulated black market for both consensual content - like porn produced in Taiwan for the Chinese market - along with stolen intimate videos, illicitly recorded voyeur content and child sex abuse material (CSAM). Last year, the Chinese state-owned Southern Daily reported on a 100,000-user-strong Telegram group named "MaskPark tree hole forum," in which men shared intimate photos and videos of their partners, along with secretly recorded footage of other women. Similar groups have also been found sharing animal abuse videos and so-called "gore" content. Such networks are not limited to China. CSAM has long been spread via private forums and chat groups, while stories like that of Gisèle Pelicot's in France have exposed horrifying cases of organized abuse in which videos are created to be shared online. The difference in China is that because all adult content is illegal, users initially seeking consensual material may be more likely to find abuse content. Huang Simin, a Chinese lawyer who specializes in sexual violence cases, said the MaskPark case "heightened the concerns of many women, as voyeuristic incidents seem to be ubiquitous." "I've noticed a general sense of powerlessness," she said, adding many felt "there's no effective way to address such incidents." Grassroots investigators like Mr. Zhou see themselves as one potential solution. Under the moniker "Rat Catcher," Mr. Zhou has made it his mission to track down such content and bring perpetrators to justice, and he's already seen tangible results. In February, after being alerted by Mr. Zhou, police in Jinan arrested the alleged ringleaders of a group recording and sharing covert footage from more than a dozen bathhouses and hot springs across China. In May, Mr. Zhou found videos being shared of primary school children in Hunan going to the bathroom; the alleged perpetrators were arrested a month later. Mr. Zhou's work is not just done online. Many of his most popular videos show him travelling to a hotel or other location where people are being covertly recorded, either to confront the alleged perpetrators or gather evidence. Often, Mr. Zhou will appear in the illicit footage in person, both to confirm where a hidden camera is located and to make himself a victim so he can file a police report. While scammers often threaten to expose illicit videos for blackmail - whether or not they have such footage - Mr. Zhou said it is rare in the cases he tracks. Blackmailing ordinary people brings with it the major risk of being caught for potentially little reward. Instead, the illegal footage itself "functions as a commercial product with layered profit channels," Mr. Zhou said. Illegal porn sites sell videos for around $7 a clip or access to live feeds of hidden cameras in hotels and changing rooms for considerably more. More often, however, Mr. Zhou said potential customers are encouraged to join private groups, paying a subscription to get access to new videos every day, like an illegal, abusive form of OnlyFans. In January, China criminalized sharing "obscene materials" online, in a broad law apparently targeted at cases like MaskPark but one free speech advocates have warned could criminalize consensual sexting. It followed a ban on installing cameras in hotel rooms, dormitories and restrooms imposed last year. Despite this, Mr. Zhou said legal loopholes remain, and the current system means people sharing videos online may face tougher punishments than those producing them in the first place. Grassroots activism remains key, he said, to stamping out illicit recording. In July, Mr. Zhou quit his job to dedicate himself full time to such work, even as his growing fame - he has more than 100,000 followers on Xiaohongshu, an Instagram-like app - has made it more difficult. "Three separate hotels have outright refused to check me in," he said. Mr. Zhou has had his government ID, address and cellphone number leaked online by criminals and often receives anonymous threats. "While the harassment is stressful, it does not break my resolve to continue," Mr. Zhou said. Importantly, he's seeing results: In the past year, Mr. Zhou said there has been a pronounced drop in the number of videos from hidden cameras in bathhouses and restrooms, something he put down to greater public awareness. "I've learned most groups have paused monetization operations," he said. "They either stopped filming entirely or are holding onto footage without distributing it online - they fear I'll trace the clips, report them to police and land them in legal trouble, making the risk far outweigh any profit."

pendingReview.title: Security expert: school camera likely 'slipped through the cracks' in Corona Del Sol case
pendingReview.description: Parents remain without many answers in the wake of the arrest of a former Tempe Union High School District employee and the subsequent voyeurism investigation at Corona Del Sol High School, sparking calls for transparency and a third-party probe. TEMPE, AZ -- Parents remain without many answers in the wake of the arrest of a former Tempe Union High School District employee and the subsequent voyeurism investigation at Corona Del Sol High School, sparking calls for transparency and a third-party probe. The district told parents a camera was inadvertently left running in the school's dance room while it was being used as a makeshift locker room, capturing students in "various states of undress," according to a police report. Investigators say 28-year-old Antony Cruz, a former district surveillance officer, downloaded footage to personal devices. He told a judge he saved the footage for documentation purposes. The district has told parents the dance room was never designated as a temporary changing room. An internal investigation into how and why that occurred is on hold as Tempe police continue to identify and contact victims, leaving the district tight-lipped in an effort to preserve the integrity of investigators' work. "It's that kind of stuff that sometimes slips through the cracks," Joe Hendry, a security consultant specializing in K-12 schools, said of the need for school staff to monitor how students use rooms where cameras are present. "Those are the kind of things the school needs to be aware of. Someone needs to be watching for that." Hendry explained that in best privacy practice, schools often install cameras outside rooms to monitor who comes in and out without capturing what happens inside--such as a camera in a hallway facing a door. The district has said the dance room camera was installed in 2024 for safety and security because the room has a door that exits outside. The district told parents there are currently no cameras in any changing areas, bathrooms, or classrooms district-wide, but there are cameras in common areas like gyms, cafeterias, weight rooms, and practice rooms. "[Common areas] should have comprehensive coverage in them," Hendry noted. "So, it shouldn't be a question that there's cameras in those areas." During Wednesday's school board meeting, a parent called for a third-party investigation into various factors surrounding the dance room camera, including who requested and approved its location, why it was installed, the scope of what it captured, who had access and why families were not informed of its installation. Superintendent Stacia Wilson acknowledged the impact the incident has had on students and families. "To the families who spoke here tonight: thank you," Dr. Wilson said. "We know it is not easy to come forward and share your concerns, and we appreciate you giving us the opportunity to listen." The superintendent said the district will share further information "as it becomes available and as we are able to do so." A Maricopa County judge entered a not-guilty plea to eight counts of voyeurism on behalf of Cruz during his arraignment. His next court date is Oct. 20 for an initial pretrial conference, with the trial scheduled to begin Dec. 31.

pendingReview.title: Smartphone LED and AI Detect Hidden Cameras
pendingReview.description: A technology has been developed to detect illegal hidden cameras in places like hotels and restrooms by simply attaching a 10,000 Korean won light-emitting diode, LED device to a smartphone. Unlike conventional methods of visually identifying lenses, AI, artificial intelligence analyzes light reflection patterns to detect camera lenses within five seconds. KAIST announced on the 30th that Professor Han Jun's team from the School of Computing, in collaboration with researchers from the National University of Singapore, NUS, and Singapore Management University, SMU, developed the smartphone-based illegal camera detection technology 'SweepLED.' The research results were presented at the international mobile computing conference 'ACM MobiSys 2026' in June. Existing portable hidden camera detectors often required users to manually identify bright spots reflected from camera lenses after illumination. This led to accuracy issues, as users frequently mistook reflections from metal, glass, or glossy plastic for camera lenses. The research team overcame these limitations with a novel approach. While keeping the smartphone camera fixed, the LED light continuously changes direction, capturing reflection changes on object surfaces. Reflections from typical glossy objects move or disappear based on the light's direction. In contrast, camera lenses exhibit unique reflection patterns when illuminated from different angles due to their internal structure of multiple lenses, apertures, and image sensors. This method analyzes the position and shape of time-varying reflections using deep learning to determine if they originate from camera lenses. Instead of identifying a single bright spot, the AI analyzes the entire pattern of changes when light is shone from multiple directions. In experiments on 30 objects commonly found in living spaces -- such as chargers, alarm clocks, remote controls, and decorations -- the technology achieved a 94% accuracy rate in detecting hidden cameras, with each inspection taking less than five seconds. The cost has also been reduced. The core component of the LED device attached to the smartphone costs around 7 dollars (approximately 10,000 Korean won). The research team expects this technology can be developed into a low-cost hidden camera detector that general consumers can carry and use like a smartphone accessory. Professor Han Jun from KAIST stated, "Illegal hidden cameras seriously threaten personal safety and privacy in everyday spaces," and added, "By combining low-cost hardware with AI analysis, we have demonstrated the potential for a detection technology that even non-experts can use easily."

pendingReview.title: [Photo] Cho Kuk and company march on prosecutors' office for probe into first lady
pendingReview.description: Cho Kuk (center), the leader of the Rebuilding Korea Party, and fellow lawmakers-elect from the party march from the Supreme Prosecutors' Office in Seoul on April 11, 2024, after holding a press event outside the office where they called for an investigation into alleged impropriety by first lady Kim Keon-hee. (Yoon Woon-sik/The Hankyoreh) In their first official act after winning their elections, Cho Kuk and fellow lawmakers-elect from the Rebuilding Korea Party marched to the Supreme Prosecutors' Office in Seoul on Thursday. Cho and other of the party's proportional representatives held a press briefing in front of the Supreme Prosecutors' Office in the capital city's Seocho District that day where they urged prosecutors to summon first lady Kim Keon-hee for questioning in relation to alleged improprieties. "We wish to relay the people's longing for judgment to be passed on Yoon Suk-yeol's prosecutorial dictatorship, which was reflected in the results of the general election, to the prosecution service," Cho said after the march. "The Korean people are asking why prosecutors are failing to investigate those who are rampantly abusing power and why the prosecution service's unforgiving scrutiny fails to target the president and his family," he added. Cho went on to touch on the Dior bag scandal that erupted surrounding the first lady's acceptance of a luxury clutch. "Do prosecutors really buy the presidential office's explanation that this was a 'spy camera sting'?" he asked. "If it were a hidden camera sting, prosecutors should subpoena those involved and punish them." The new party's leader went on to say that if prosecutors failed to "follow the commands of the people," he and his party would work together with the Democratic Party to quickly pursue legislation assigning special counsel to the cases surrounding Kim Keon-hee once the 22nd National Assembly kicks off. "If prosecutors don't take action and investigate, the first lady will face a subpoena and questioning from a special counsel," he said. Following their press conference, Cho and the other lawmakers-elect marched from the gate of the Supreme Prosecutors' Office to outside the Supreme Court while carrying signs that read "Subpoena first lady Kim Keon-hee." By Yoon Woon-sik, senior staff writer
